The paper analyzes the steady-state entropy production rate (EPR) of active scalar φ4 field theories near Ising critical points.
The authors consider both nonconserved (Active Model A) and conserved (Active Model B) dynamics at the Gaussian level, as well as the nonconserved case (Active Model A) to leading order in ε = 4-d.
Near the Gaussian fixed point, the critical EPR scales as σ ~ ξ^-(d+z) ~ t^ν(d+z), where ξ is the correlation length, t is the reduced temperature, and z is the dynamic critical exponent.

For Active Model A near the Wilson-Fisher fixed point in d=4-ε dimensions, the critical EPR scales as σ ~ ξ^-(d+z-ε/12) ~ t^-νε/12, indicating that the critical EPR is much larger in magnitude than the natural scaling would suggest.
The authors introduce the concept of 'stealth entropy production', where the critical EPR remains significant even when the active terms are irrelevant in the renormalization group (RG) sense.

The calculation for the critical EPR near the Wilson-Fisher fixed point involves two stages: finding the RG flow of the coupling constants λ and κ_1, and then calculating the scaling of the composite operators that they multiply.
The sign of the critical EPR σ is not guaranteed to be positive, and the authors note that the negativity of σ in some parameter regions requires further study and interpretation.

The authors suggest that further studies, including numerical investigations, are needed to clarify the character and interpretation of the steady-state EPR close to the critical points of active field theories.

The authors find that the nontrivial critical scaling of the EPR should be viewed as a universal dynamic Ising-class property, rather than an indication that the active models become effectively passive at criticality.

The positive scaling exponent θ_σ = νε/12 + O(ε^2) found near the Wilson-Fisher fixed point suggests that the critical EPR may exhibit anomalous scaling or fractal properties close to equilibrium-like fixed points.
The authors note that the choice of coupling constants g_i = (λ, λ+κ_1) in the decomposition of the EPR is motivated by the fact that these pairs do not mix in the RG flow.
The calculation of the anomalous dimensions of the composite operators in the EPR expression involves mixing between operators of the same dimension, which is a complication that must be addressed.
The authors state that in d=2, where the active terms are not irrelevant, the measure needed to evaluate the EPR expression is not known, limiting the progress that can be made in that case.
The authors suggest that the physics of a divergent reduced entropy production, ψ ~ t^-θ_σ with θ_σ > 0, is not yet clear and merits further study.

The authors note that any equilibrium system has a vanishing EPR, so their results only provide information about a system whose activity is strictly nonzero, while remaining irrelevant in the RG sense.
